strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open question: whether the empirically observed generalization gap between Byzantine and data-poisoning attacks in robust distributed learning is fundamental or an artifact of suboptimal attacks. This is the first paper to give a theoretical (rather than purely empirical) account of this gap.

The technical approach is sound and comprehensive: the paper derives upper bounds on uniform stability for both threat models across convex, strongly convex, and smooth nonconvex regimes, and crucially complements the Byzantine-case upper bound with a matching (up to constants) lower bound for the poisoning case using SMEA, establishing tightness of the O(f/(n-f)) vs O(sqrt(f/(n-2f))) gap.

The proof technique is well-motivated and clearly explained: for Byzantine attacks, an intermediate comparison to the honest averaging update is introduced because adversarial vectors cannot be assumed to respect any regularity, whereas for poisoning attacks the true co-coercivity/smoothness of the (corrupted-but-still valid) loss can be exploited directly, giving tighter bounds. This mechanistic explanation is intuitive and well supported by the formal analysis (e.g., via the CWTM/SMEA subset-selection argument and violation of co-coercivity).

The paper connects the stability gap to generalization error directly via a concrete closed-form example (Section 4, Appendix E.2), and validates the theoretical upper bounds numerically, including designing a tailored/adaptive Byzantine attack that empirically matches the theoretical worst case, lending credibility to the claimed tightness.

The related work section carefully differentiates the contribution from prior works (Farhadkhani et al. on optimization error equivalence, Farhadkhani et al. on PAC learning equivalence, Ye & Ling on decentralized SGD stability), clarifying why those results do not resolve or contradict this paper's claims.

Extensive appendix material (properties of CWTM/SMEA, refined bounds under bounded heterogeneity/variance, high-probability excess risk bounds) suggests care taken toward rigor and completeness, and the writing of proofs is detailed enough to be largely reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: The headline lower bound (Theorem 3.3, matching Theorem 3.2) is established only for SMEA and only in a very specific, adversarially constructed toy scenario (three collinear-gradient subgroups, a single pivot worker, essentially 1-D constructions even when 'generalized' to R^d). While the authors argue the underlying mechanism (failure to preserve co-coercivity) is generic, no lower bound is given for CWTM in the convex setting (acknowledged as an open technical gap, Remark D.2/D.3), leaving the generality of the claimed fundamental gap only partially established.

The numerical validation (Section 4, Figure 1) is on a small, essentially degenerate synthetic problem (n=15, linear/toy loss, T=5, GD only, no real datasets, no stochastic noise/variance reported) directly instantiating the same construction used for the lower-bound proof. This is circular in the sense that it validates the theory on the exact adversarial construction designed to prove the theory, rather than providing independent empirical evidence (e.g., realistic heterogeneous data, real robust-learning benchmarks) that the gap manifests in practical robust distributed learning systems.

The 'tailored Byzantine attack' used to empirically demonstrate worse instability is hand-crafted with knowledge of the SMEA selection mechanism and the specific problem instance (Appendix E.1); it is unclear how representative or generalizable this attack is beyond the constructed toy setting, and no comparison is made against a broad suite of known Byzantine attacks (e.g., ALIE, IPM, etc.) on more standard benchmarks.

The nonconvex results (Theorem 3.4 vs 3.5) exhibit an unresolved gap: the CWTM poisoning bound has a sqrt(n) dependence instead of n for f=0, explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'a proof artifact,' undermining the tightness claims in the nonconvex regime and leaving the comparison between Byzantine and poisoning stability in the nonconvex case less conclusive than in the convex case.

The practical implications discussion (ZKPs preventing Byzantine failures) is somewhat tangential/speculative and not rigorously connected to the paper's formal results; it reads more as motivating narrative than a substantiated contribution.

The paper's scope is restricted to specific robust aggregation rules (SMEA and CWTM) satisfying a particular (f,κ,·)-robustness definition; it is not established whether the qualitative Byzantine-vs-poisoning gap generalizes to other robust aggregators (e.g., median-based, Krum, etc.), somewhat limiting the generality of the 'fundamental' claim in the title/abstract.

Presentation is dense with heavy notational overhead which, combined with results being scattered across a large appendix, may hinder accessibility for readers who are not already deeply familiar with this specific line of robust-distributed-learning literature.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and previously open theoretical question: why Byzantine failures empirically generalize worse than data poisoning despite prior results showing comparable optimization guarantees. The paper convincingly explains this gap via a stability-based analysis.

Rigorous theory with matching (up to log/constant factors) upper and lower bounds on uniform stability for data poisoning (Theorems 3.3, 3.4), and a non-trivial lower bound for Byzantine failures (Theorem 3.2) in the regime f in [n/3, n/2), establishing a genuine order-of-magnitude separation between the two threat models.

Technically interesting proof machinery, notably Lemma D.1 characterizing the SMEA aggregation rule's behavior on collinear gradient vectors, which is reused across several lower-bound constructions and could be of independent interest for future robust-aggregation analyses.

The paper connects stability bounds to actual generalization error (not just an upper bound but a matching construction, Lemma 4.1/Theorem 4.2), and its numerical experiment (Figure 1) corroborates the theoretical predictions, including matching constants under data poisoning.

Clear, honest discussion of limitations and open questions (Section H and future work list): the paper explicitly notes that the tight Byzantine lower bound only holds for f ≥ n/3, that other aggregation rules/algorithms (momentum, multi-step methods) are not formally analyzed, and discusses why optimization vs. generalization differ conceptually.
Reasonably thorough related-work positioning, clarifying differences from Farhadkhani et al. (2024b), Farhadkhani et al. (2022b), and Ye & Ling (2025).
weaknesses: The headline claim of a 'fundamental gap' is rigorously established only for f in [n/3, n/2); for the practically important regime f < n/3, the paper has no matching Byzantine lower bound and relies solely on limited numerical evidence (Section 4) to argue the gap persists, which weakens the generality of the central claim.

Nearly all tightness results (both upper and lower bounds) are specific to the SMEA aggregation rule; while the paper argues some proof ideas generalize, the concrete matching-bound results do not obviously extend to other widely used robust aggregators (e.g., trimmed mean, Krum, CClip), limiting the scope of the 'fundamental' separation claim.

Empirical validation is very limited: a single small-scale (n=15) synthetic instantiation that essentially replicates the exact worst-case construction used in the theoretical proofs, rather than independent experiments on realistic datasets/models with standard/adaptive attacks; this makes it hard to assess how much the gap manifests in practical (non-worst-case) distributed learning settings.

The stability constructions rely on quite pathological loss functions and point-mass/two-point data distributions (e.g., linear losses, Dirac mixtures) that are common in the stability-analysis literature but are far from realistic loss landscapes, making it less clear how tightly these theoretical rates predict practical generalization gaps for, e.g., deep networks.

The paper does not formally extend results to momentum-based, variance-reduced, or multi-local-step algorithms (FedAvg-style), which are the most practically relevant distributed learning methods; these are deferred to future work with only informal arguments in the appendix.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy even by theory-paper standards, which may limit accessibility; some intuitive explanations (e.g., 'why optimization is unaffected but generalization is') would benefit from earlier, more prominent placement in the main text rather than being pushed to Section 4/discussion.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open question: prior work (Farhadkhani et al. 2024b) showed comparable optimization guarantees between Byzantine failures and data poisoning, yet empirical studies consistently report worse generalization under Byzantine attacks. This paper is the first to attempt a rigorous, stability-based theoretical explanation for this gap.

The data poisoning upper and lower bounds (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4) are tight and match at rate Θ(f/(n-f)), giving a genuinely satisfying closed-form characterization for that threat model, together with a clean intuition (failure of aggregation rules to preserve co-coercivity).

The paper connects its stability results to an explicit, non-trivial generalization gap (Theorem 4.2) rather than only comparing stability upper bounds, and supports the theory with a numerical experiment that tracks the derived bounds closely.

The technical machinery (Lemma D.1 characterizing SMEA on collinear vectors, the general co-coercivity-violation argument) is a reusable proof technique that could be of independent interest for future stability analyses of robust aggregation rules.

Extensive appendix with careful, mostly self-contained proofs, and a thoughtful discussion section addressing why optimization and generalization differ, plus candid discussion of open questions and limitations (Section H).
weaknesses: The paper's central claim of a 'fundamental gap' is only rigorously established for f ≥ n/3. For the arguably more practically relevant low-to-moderate misbehaving-worker regime f < n/3, the authors have only a weaker upper bound and rely on numerical experiments (Figure 1) to argue the gap persists; the paper explicitly acknowledges this as an open question rather than a proven result, which undercuts the strength of the title's assertion.

All matching lower bounds (both Byzantine and data poisoning) rely on very specific, hand-crafted 1D (or thin 2D) linear/piecewise loss constructions with carefully engineered Dirac-like or two-point data distributions. While mathematically valid as worst-case constructions, it is unclear how representative these pathological examples are of realistic heterogeneous distributed learning, limiting the practical significance of the 'fundamental' framing.

The analysis is restricted to (strongly) convex, Lipschitz, smooth losses and to a single aggregation rule (SMEA) for the tight results; GD/SGD with a single local step per round is analyzed, while modern practice (deep non-convex models, momentum, multiple local steps as in FedAvg) is left to informal discussion (Section H) without any formal guarantees or even sketch proofs.

The empirical validation is purely synthetic (T=5, n=15, a linear loss, m=1), directly instantiating the theoretical worst-case construction; there is no experiment on realistic datasets/networks to demonstrate that the predicted gap manifests in practical settings, so the connection between the theory and the motivating empirical literature (e.g., Allouah et al. 2023a Table 2) remains indirect.

The generalization result in Section 4 (Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2) is derived under the restrictive assumption m=1 (single sample per honest worker) and reuses the exact worst-case datasets from the stability lower bounds, so it does not provide additional independent evidence beyond what the stability bounds already imply.

Some claims of generality (e.g., 'This result generalizes beyond SMEA, yielding the same upper bounds for any rule that averages n−f gradients') are stated without a fully worked out proof for general aggregation rules beyond SMEA, and the extension to other algorithms (momentum, variance reduction) is deferred entirely to informal discussion.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open question: whether the empirically observed generalization gap between Byzantine failures and data poisoning is fundamental or merely an artifact of suboptimal attacks. The paper provides the first rigorous theoretical resolution of this question.

Technically strong contribution: derives matching (tight) upper and lower bounds Θ(f/(n-f)) on uniform stability under data poisoning for SMEA, and a lower bound Ω(√(f/(n-2f))) under Byzantine failures for f≥n/3, establishing an order-of-magnitude separation between the two threat models.

Goes beyond the standard one-directional stability→generalization bound by constructing an explicit setting (Lemma 4.1) where generalization error is *proportional* to stability, allowing the stability gap to be translated into a genuine generalization gap (Theorem 4.2), which is a more convincing argument than relying on upper bounds alone.

Careful, technically detailed proofs (extensive appendix) with clever constructions (e.g., adaptive Byzantine triggering, worker-swapping arguments for SMEA) that are well explained via proof sketches in the main text.

Good positioning relative to closely related work (Farhadkhani et al. 2022b, 2024b; Ye and Ling 2025), clearly explaining why prior equivalence results do not contradict this paper's separation result.

Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical bounds, including matching constants in the data-poisoning regime, and illustrate that the gap persists even outside the region with proven lower bounds (f<n/3).

Honest and thorough discussion of limitations and future directions (Sections 4 and H), including the open regime f<n/3, extension to other optimizers (momentum, local steps), and other threat models (locally-poisonous, backdoor attacks).
Practical relevance is discussed (e.g., motivating the use of zero-knowledge proofs against Byzantine but not data-poisoning attacks), adding some real-world grounding to the theory.
weaknesses: The core lower bound separating Byzantine failures from data poisoning is only proven for f≥n/3; for f<n/3, which is arguably the more practically relevant regime, the paper only provides numerical evidence, leaving the central claim of a 'fundamental gap' incompletely established theoretically in this regime.

Results are largely specific to the SMEA aggregation rule (though the paper argues some generalize to other (f,κ)-robust rules that average n-f gradients); it is unclear how tight/representative these bounds are for other widely used robust aggregators (e.g., trimmed mean, Krum) that behave differently from SMEA.

Analysis is restricted to GD/SGD; extensions to momentum-based or multi-local-step methods (e.g., FedAvg) commonly used in practice are left as future work, so the practical scope of the fundamental gap claim is somewhat narrower than the framing in the abstract/introduction might suggest.

The lower-bound constructions rely on highly specific, worst-case data distributions and loss functions (e.g., piecewise-linear/linear losses, Dirac-supported distributions), which, while standard practice for stability lower bounds, may make it harder to intuit how broadly the separation manifests under more realistic heterogeneous data and losses beyond the numerical validation provided.

The paper's numerous nested regimes and dense technical machinery (multiple theorems, sub-cases based on parity of n-f, thresholds on f relative to n/3, n/2) make the presentation demanding, and some connections between the main text and the lengthy appendix proofs could be made more accessible.
